raw:
{
  "need": "Identity",
  "secondary": { "name": "Status", "description": "Admitting struggle feels like losing the reputation they have worked hard to build with you and the team." },
  "read": "Their identity is wrapped up in being the person who handles everything and never cracks. Saying they are fine is not dishonesty — it is self-protection. Acknowledging the workload would mean admitting a limit, and right now that feels like erasing the thing that makes them matter here.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Quietly pull work off their plate or stop assigning them anything hard — it feels kind but signals you have lost confidence in them, which is the opposite of what they need and quietly confirms their fear that admitting struggle means losing status." },
  "mentorMove": "Hold the standard that sustainable performance is a real job requirement, not a soft preference, while making it safe to tell the truth by treating honesty about capacity as a sign of professionalism, not weakness.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "Sustainable output is a standard, not a perk — you will not quietly watch them run themselves into the ground.",
    "The expectation is that they communicate capacity honestly so the team can plan around reality, not around the story they are telling."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "How they restore capacity is up to them — redistributing tasks, adjusting deadlines, blocking focus time, or something else entirely.",
    "The conversation can happen over coffee, in a one-on-one, or in a short async note — whatever format lowers the social stakes for them."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I want to check in with you — not as a performance thing, just as someone who pays attention. You have been carrying a lot and I see how hard you have been working." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "I am not going to pretend I have the full picture, so I want to ask directly: when you say you are fine, what does fine actually look like for you right now? Walk me through a typical week." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is what I know: the best people I have worked with are not the ones who never hit a wall — they are the ones who know how to manage through it. I want us to look at your load together and figure out what actually makes sense, because running at 110 percent for too long costs the team more than it saves." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I am holding you to a high standard here, and part of that standard is performing in a way you can sustain. I know you can do that — I would not be having this conversation if I did not believe it. So let us land on one concrete adjustment before we wrap up today." }
  ],
  "longGame": "Over the next few weeks, normalize capacity conversations in every one-on-one so honesty about limits becomes part of your culture with them, not a one-time intervention. The goal is that they start to see managing their own bandwidth as a professional skill they are developing, not a confession they have to make."
}
situation: One of my best people is clearly overworked and heading for burnout but insists they are fine.
